vignette:
Mina, a 24-year-old South Eastern Asian woman working as an urban planner in a busy city office, grew up with a father who used physical punishment at home in ways that left her feeling controlled, humiliated, and powerless. She did not talk about those years easily. Even now, when she tried to deliberately remember what happened, the details felt strangely out of reach, as if her mind shut a door before she could grasp what was behind it. What came back more readily was not a clear scene but a rush of emotion: sudden rage, a hot, full-body surge that seemed to arrive without warning, and at times the same emotional intensity without any clear image at all. When she was asked about the past, she could only say that what happened was deeply unfair and that nothing had ever been done about it; beneath that was a quieter conviction that she had been weak, the kind of person bad things happened to. The more she sat with these thoughts, the more she felt as if she had been treated like an object rather than a person, handled and acted upon without choice. In moments of recollection, that anger and those appraisals fed directly into her efforts to put the memory away, to change the subject, to keep herself from being reminded of it by other people, and to go along with whatever others wanted so she could feel safe.

Those reactions became especially pronounced around anything medical. During a recent appointment for a routine physical, when the nurse asked her to roll up her sleeve and lie back for the examination, Mina felt her body tighten before the procedure had even begun. Being seen in that exposed, scrutinized way made her feel watched and helpless, and the nausea that rose in her stomach had become one of the clearest signals that she was not safe. The sensation brought back the same unrehearsed emotional surge she sometimes felt without images, and at other times it dragged up fragments so quickly she could not hold onto them. Her mind immediately turned toward the injustice of it all, the sense that she had been made into something to be handled, and she was left with the belief that she was weak for still reacting this way as an adult. In those moments she would comply automatically, nodding, smiling, and doing whatever the clinician asked without question, hoping that pleasing them would keep the experience brief and prevent any attention from lingering on her. She later noticed the same pattern at work when colleagues suggested health screenings or when a client meeting was held in a medical office building; she would agree too quickly, then spend the rest of the day feeling as if she had betrayed herself.

Over the months, Mina's world narrowed around safety in only a very limited number of places. Her apartment, one corner of the office, and the back seat of a rideshare at night felt tolerable; everywhere else carried the sense that something could happen at any moment. Sudden movements by others put her immediately on guard, especially in crowded transit stations and open-plan meetings where a hand reaching across a table or someone standing too quickly could jolt her into a hard alertness. That alertness made concentration difficult, and she described losing the thread of design discussions at work because part of her was always watching the room. The more she stayed on guard, the more she found herself trying to reduce exposure: declining lunches, avoiding reminders of the past when relatives brought up family discipline, and arranging her schedule around escape routes and predictable environments. Yet those strategies also kept the memory alive in an unhelpful way. When she tried to push it away or keep people pleased, she felt more distant from herself, and the same old belief that she was an object, not a person, returned with fresh force. On days when she spent hours bracing for threat, a small comment or a casual movement could suddenly become a trigger, and the body memory of fear would surface before any picture did. In turn, those bodily surges and the inability to retrieve the memory clearly made her more certain that something terrible and unresolved still lived in her, which deepened her sense of danger and kept her scanning. She began to feel that she was failing both at work and in relationships, always accommodating others while privately believing she was fundamentally weak and unprotected.

Mina finally sought help after an especially difficult week in which a medical screening at work, a nausea spell on the train, and an unexpectedly fast movement from a coworker left her shaking and unable to concentrate on a project deadline. She was increasingly afraid that she would keep shrinking her life until there were almost no places that felt safe at all. At the same time, she hoped that therapy might help her make sense of the rage, the fragmentary memories, and the way ordinary situations had come to feel dangerous, and that she might learn how to live as a person in her own life rather than as someone perpetually bracing to be handled.
